subUnits.title: 6.1 Rhyme, Rhythm, and Metre
notes: Rhyme, Rhythm, and Metre
Key Concepts:
1. RHYME:
- The repetition of similar sounds at the END of lines (end rhyme) or within lines (internal rhyme).
- RHYME SCHEME: the pattern of end rhymes, labelled with letters (e.g., ABAB, ABCABC).
- PERFECT RHYME: identical vowel and final consonant sounds (e.g., 'cat/hat').
- SLANT RHYME (half rhyme): approximate rhyme — similar but not identical sounds (e.g., 'worm/farm').
2. RHYTHM:
- The musical beat or pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables in poetry.
- Even without strict metre, most poems have a recognisable rhythmic flow.
3. METRE:
- The formal, measurable pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables in a line.
- Common metrical feet: IAMB (da-DUM), TROCHEE (DUM-da), ANAPEST (da-da-DUM), DACTYL (DUM-da-da).
- Lines named by number of feet: PENTAMETER (5 feet), TETRAMETER (4 feet), HEXAMETER (6 feet).
Common Mistakes:
- Do NOT confuse RHYME SCHEME with RHYTHM — rhyme scheme is the pattern of end sounds; rhythm is the beat.
- Do NOT assume metre is the same as rhythm — metre is the formal, counted pattern; rhythm is the overall musical flow.

quiz.q: END RHYME in poetry refers to:
opts: Rhyming words within the same line
The repetition of similar sounds at the end of lines
The beat pattern of syllables
An approximate, near-rhyme
quiz.explanation: End rhyme occurs when the last words of lines share similar sounds, creating a sense of completion and musicality.

opts: Identical vowel and consonant sounds
No relationship between words' sounds
Approximate rhyme — similar but not identical sounds
Rhyming words within the same line
quiz.explanation: Slant rhyme creates an imperfect, approximate echo of sound — close enough to feel rhyme-like but not an exact match.

opts: The beat pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables
The pattern of end rhymes in a poem, labelled with letters
The number of syllables in each line
The emotional tone of the poem
quiz.explanation: A rhyme scheme maps out the pattern of rhyming line endings using letter labels (A, B, C, etc.).

opts: The formal, counted metrical pattern only
The pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables creating a musical beat
The rhyme scheme of the poem
The length of the poem
quiz.explanation: Rhythm is the underlying musical pulse of a poem — the pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables giving it movement.

quiz.q: METRE differs from rhythm in that metre:
opts: Is informal and uncounted
Is the formal, measurable, counted pattern of syllables — rhythm is the overall musical feel
Only applies to prose
Is the same as rhyme scheme
quiz.explanation: Metre is the strict, counted formal pattern; rhythm is the broader musical effect created by the poem's syllable patterns.

opts: 4 dactylic feet per line
5 iambic feet per line (da-DUM x 5 = 10 syllables)
3 trochaic feet per line
6 anapestic feet per line
quiz.explanation: Iambic pentameter has five iambs (da-DUM) per line, totalling 10 syllables — the most common metre in English poetry.

quiz.q: A TROCHEE is a metrical foot consisting of:
opts: An unstressed followed by a stressed syllable (da-DUM)
A stressed followed by two unstressed syllables (DUM-da-da)
Two unstressed followed by one stressed syllable (da-da-DUM)
A stressed followed by an unstressed syllable (DUM-da)
quiz.explanation: A trochee reverses the iamb — it is a stressed syllable followed by an unstressed one (DUM-da).

opts: Words at the end of two different lines rhyme
A word within a line rhymes with another word within the same or adjacent line
No words in the poem rhyme
Only the first and last lines rhyme
quiz.explanation: Internal rhyme places rhyming words inside lines rather than only at their ends, creating additional musical texture.

opts: Four feet
Five feet
Six feet
Seven feet
quiz.explanation: Penta- means five — pentameter lines contain five metrical feet.

opts: Slant rhyme
Internal rhyme only
Perfect (exact) rhyme
No rhyme
quiz.explanation: 'Cat' and 'hat' share identical vowel (a) and final consonant (t) sounds — making them a perfect rhyme.

subUnits.title: 6.2 Stanza, Poetic Licence, and Poetic Persona
notes: Stanza, Poetic Licence, and Poetic Persona
Key Concepts:
1. STANZA:
- A grouped set of lines within a poem, separated by a blank line — the poem's equivalent of a paragraph.
- Named by number of lines: COUPLET (2), TERCET (3), QUATRAIN (4), QUINTET (5), SESTET (6), OCTET (8).
2. POETIC LICENCE:
- The freedom a poet takes to deviate from standard grammar, spelling, syntax, or factual accuracy for artistic effect.
- Examples: inverted word order ('silent the forest grew'), non-standard punctuation, invented words.
3. POETIC PERSONA:
- The speaker constructed by the poet for a poem — the 'I' of the poem.
- The persona may be very different from the poet — it can be a historical figure, a fictional character, or a voice the poet invents.
- Understanding the persona is essential to interpreting the poem's meaning and tone.
Common Mistakes:
- Do NOT confuse STANZA with VERSE — 'verse' can refer to a single line or to poetry generally; 'stanza' specifically refers to a grouped set of lines.
- Do NOT assume POETIC LICENCE means a poet can write anything carelessly — it is a deliberate artistic choice, not an excuse for bad writing.

opts: A single line of a poem
An individual word chosen carefully by the poet
A grouped set of lines within a poem, separated by a blank line
The entire poem as a whole
quiz.explanation: A stanza is a grouped set of lines — the structural unit of a poem, equivalent to a paragraph in prose.

quiz.q: A QUATRAIN is a stanza of:
opts: Two lines
Three lines
Four lines
Six lines
quiz.explanation: A quatrain has four lines — it is the most common stanza form in English poetry.

opts: Two lines, often rhyming
Four lines
Six lines
Eight lines
quiz.explanation: A couplet is a two-line stanza — in many traditions, the lines rhyme with each other.

opts: A formal qualification earned by poets
The freedom to deviate from standard grammar or syntax for deliberate artistic effect
The legal right to publish poems
Following all rules of standard English perfectly
quiz.explanation: Poetic licence is the artistic freedom to break language conventions when doing so serves the poem's meaning or beauty.

quiz.q: An example of poetic licence is:
opts: Using perfect standard grammar throughout
Copying another poem exactly
Writing 'silent the forest grew' instead of 'the forest grew silent' — inverting word order for effect
Avoiding all figurative language
quiz.explanation: Inverted word order (hyperbaton) is a common use of poetic licence — placing emphasis and creating rhythmic variety.

opts: Always the poet themselves
The speaker constructed by the poet for the poem — who may differ greatly from the poet
The main character of the poem's narrative
The audience addressed by the poem
quiz.explanation: The persona is the voice of the poem — a literary construct that may be very different from the biographical poet.

quiz.q: Understanding the persona of a poem is important because:
opts: It reveals the poet's exact personal biography
It is irrelevant to interpretation
It helps the reader interpret the poem's tone, viewpoint, and meaning correctly
The persona is always obvious and needs no analysis
quiz.explanation: Knowing who is speaking, from what position, and with what emotional stance is essential to correct poetic interpretation.

quiz.q: A SESTET is a stanza of:
opts: Four lines
Five lines
Six lines
Eight lines
quiz.explanation: A sestet has six lines — it forms the second part of a Petrarchan sonnet.

quiz.q: Poetic licence is NOT an excuse for careless writing because:
opts: Poets never break rules
It is a deliberate artistic choice made for specific effect — not accidental poor writing
All grammar rules can always be freely broken
Good poems never use standard grammar
quiz.explanation: Poetic licence is intentional — every deliberate deviation from convention should serve a clear artistic purpose.

quiz.q: An OCTET is a stanza of:
opts: Four lines
Six lines
Seven lines
Eight lines
quiz.explanation: An octet has eight lines — it forms the first part of a Petrarchan sonnet.
